On 4 December 1829 the governor general of India, Lord William Bentinck, made sati, the burning or burying alive of a widow with her husband's body, a crime in the Bengal Presidency.

Sati was never common, but in Bengal in the early 1800s hundreds of cases a year were recorded. The East India Company had long avoided touching Hindu customs, fearing unrest. Reformers pushed it to act, above all Ram Mohan Roy, who argued from the old texts that the scriptures did not require it, and who saw his own sister in law burned.

The law made helping at a sati culpable homicide. Orthodox Hindus in Calcutta formed the Dharma Sabha and appealed to the Privy Council in London, which rejected their case in 1832. Similar rules followed in Madras and Bombay in 1830.

The ban did not end sati at once, and a case as late as 1987 led to a new law in independent India. But it set a pattern: Indian reformers and British law joining to change family custom. The Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 followed the same path.
sum: On 4 December 1829 the governor general of India, Lord William Bentinck, made sati, the burning or burying alive of a widow with her husband's body, a crime in the Bengal Presidency.
